title: Factorising Expressions

findings.finding: Compare different supplied factors for the same expression.
findings.breakdown: Holding the expression fixed exposes how the supplied outside factor changes the coefficients inside the brackets.
findings.checked: The proposed factorisations are correct and require only the division method taught in p4-factorising-method. Existing practice does not hold an expression fixed while varying its supplied factor. The sequence adds only one prediction instruction.
findings.assumptions: Factors are supplied, as throughout Factorising 1; students need not select an HCF.

repair.proposal: After p5-q1-o, append: 'Predict how the numbers inside the brackets will change.' (p) 12x+18=2(...); answer: 2(6x+9). (q) 12x+18=3(...); answer: 3(4x+6). (r) 12x+18=6(...); answer: 6(2x+3). Follow with the unpatterned part (s) 15x-20=5(...); answer: 5(3x-4).

findings.doneWhen: The three comparison parts and one unpatterned part appear under the existing instruction, with only the prediction line added.

findings.finding: The unequal-denominator demonstration does not show how the outside factor 5/6 was selected.
findings.breakdown: Expanding the supplied product verifies it but leaves the forward decision unmodelled: obtaining a common denominator and then taking a common factor from the numerator. Part b immediately requires students to make that decision.
findings.checked: Earlier teaching models numerical and algebraic common factors. p16-q19 introduces fractional factors only with equal denominators. No preceding teaching or practice demonstrates selecting a fractional factor when denominators differ. The proposed connecting calculation is correct.
findings.assumptions: Equivalent fractions are prior knowledge. Selecting a fractional factor for unequal denominators is the new variant; no calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: After p17-q20-a and before part b, add: 'First use a common denominator: 5x/3+5y/6=(10x+5y)/6. The numerator has common factor 5, so this equals (5/6)(2x+y). Use the same approach below.'

findings.doneWhen: The demonstration connects the original denominators and numerators to the selected factor before students construct their own factorisations.

history.note: Its comment was deleted in Studio.

findings.finding: q22 introduces testing an identity through incompatible coefficient conditions without showing that method.
findings.breakdown: Students must recognise that one constant must satisfy both coefficient conditions. Finding a value from just one condition produces an incorrect conclusion, and preceding instruction does not explain how to check compatibility.
findings.checked: Earlier material teaches expansion, factorisation and a single linear equation; q21 matches one common multiplier. None demonstrates incompatible conditions for an identity. Expanding q22-a requires k=3 and k=2 simultaneously; q22-b requires k=4 and k=3 simultaneously. Both therefore have no constant solution. Its closing position does not supply the new identity-testing method.
findings.assumptions: Expansion and simple linear equations are available prior knowledge; coefficient comparison for identities has not been taught in the supplied complete teaching.

repair.proposal: Before q22, add: 'For an equation to hold for every value of the variable, coefficients of matching powers must agree. For example, kx(x+2)=3x²+8x expands to kx²+2kx=3x²+8x. The x² coefficients require k=3; the x coefficients require 2k=8, giving k=4. These conflict, so no constant k works.'

findings.doneWhen: Students see how to derive and compare both conditions before attempting q22.

findings.finding: Use the existing rectangle area to compare alternative pairs of dimensions.
findings.breakdown: Different choices of outside factor connect equivalent products with rectangles of equal area.
findings.checked: The extension follows an existing practice question and uses its area expression. Both symbolic widths are correct. At a=2 the area is 24, and all three stated dimension pairs have product 24. Only previously taught factorisation and substitution are needed.
findings.assumptions: The original rectangle context supplies positive dimensions, hence a>2/3; the proposed rectangles are valid throughout that domain.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts to p15-q11: (b) 'A rectangle with the same area has length 3. Find its width.' Answer: 3a²-2a. (c) 'A rectangle with the same area has length a. Find its width.' Answer: 9a-6. (d) 'If a=2, give the length and width of each of the three rectangles.' Answers: original rectangle 6 by 4; part b rectangle 3 by 8; part c rectangle 2 by 12.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up parts retain the original area and compare the three correct pairs of dimensions.
